open_obligations: Check whether skeptical-prior judges were ever shown a false claim matching their prior, the exact case Irving et al. describe.
Note the debaters are GPT-4o; check what sources they use and whether they are trained.
Check whether the skeptical-judge subgroup is large enough to detect an effect.
in.other_title: Debate 70.1% vs consultancy 60.0% final human judge accuracy
in.rationale: Irving et al. worry that a false opening the human already believes may win because of belief bias. Rahman et al. compare judges with mainstream or skeptical prior beliefs and report debate raising accuracy from 63.2% to 70.1% versus consultancy 61.4% to 60.0%, with a 15.2% advantage for mainstream-prior judges but only a non-significant 4.7% (p = 0.2) for skeptical-prior judges.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate still helps human judges who hold mainstream or skeptical prior beliefs, on COVID-19 factuality claims with GPT-4o debaters

text: The authors worry that if Alice opens with a false statement the human already believes, Bob's refutation may rest on premises both agents accept but the human does not, and note humans are subject to belief bias. They say the PSPACE argument indicates that there is some threshold of judge performance beyond which debate is practically limited only by capacity, and ask whether humans are above that threshold.
title: Human judge belief bias may let a false but already-believed opening win
